angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
subject: A rainstick held across the screen, modelled as a hollow tube with a cord grip, growth nodes and pins driven through it in a spiral, where each ring of pins is a course and the pin a falling pebble just struck rings with light at its head.
controls: rate: how many pin heads carry a ring (count: recently struck pins, about 4 at 1.0 a beat to about 20 at 8), the newest filled bright.
roof: how many rings of pins the stick has (count, 1 ring at 0 st to 22 at 36 st), spaced evenly along the same tube, so a flat roof is a stick with one ring of pins.
gust: the stick tips (rotation about its centre, ±25° from its rest angle): tipped one way the struck pins run in order down the tube (falling runs), the other way up; at 0 the strikes scatter.
puddle: pebbles gathered in the open mouth at the near end (count, 0 to ~8 small closed outlines visible inside the rim), the ones that will be poured back through as replays.
reference: library/theseus-tower (a 3D object drawn as detailed line art from one camera; only what plays lights)
risks: Pin heads are 4 px dots at 1:1: right at the size floor; struck rings make them readable but the unstruck spiral is faint.
Tipping is an in-plane turn of the whole tube, so the 3D yaw stays fixed; at ±25° the ends approach the header and frame edge and the camera fit has to leave room.
The rainstick is a rain instrument, not a roof: the 'roof' label maps to pin rings, which is the right idea but a new picture for the name.
Pins on the hidden side of the tube can't show a strike; strikes must be drawn on visible pins only, which biases which notes look played.
Muted: the stick lies at rest angle, no rings, the mouth empty and its rim dims to G3.
